passages.happening:
“Now Sarah lived to be 127 years old” (verse 1).

“She died in Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron) in the land of Canaan, and Abraham went out to mourn and to weep for her” (verse 2).
passages.hearers:
Two short verses close a long life. Sarah left Ur and Haran with Abraham. She lived in tents for decades. She was taken into the houses of two kings and rescued twice. She waited for a child until she laughed at the idea, and then she laughed for joy. Now she dies.

Isaac was born when Sarah was ninety (17:17). So he is about thirty-seven when she dies.

Hebron lies in the hill country of Judah, south of Jerusalem. Its older name, Kiriath-arba, means ‘town of Arba’ (Joshua 14:15). Abraham had long camped nearby, by the oaks of Mamre (13:18).

Abraham mourns and weeps. The man who rose early to obey God in the last chapter now sits beside his dead wife and cries. Faith and grief are not enemies. The father of faith weeps.
passages.later:
Jesus himself weeps at the grave of his friend Lazarus: “Jesus wept” (John 11:35). Paul does not tell Christians not to grieve. He tells them not to “grieve like the rest, who are without hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13).

Isaiah tells Israel to remember her: “Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah who gave you birth” (Isaiah 51:2). Peter holds Sarah up as a woman who hoped in God (1 Peter 3:5-6), and Hebrews names her among the faithful (Hebrews 11:11).
passages.hard: A word of care. Some readers come to this chapter grieving a husband, a wife, a parent or a friend. Abraham's tears were not a lack of faith, and yours are not either. If your grief is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a grief counsellor. If the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Abraham, who had trusted God through everything, sat down and wept for his wife. Ask whether you have let yourself grieve, or whether you think faith means not crying. Then remember that the father of faith wept, and so did Jesus.

passages.t: ‘I am a foreigner and an outsider among you’
passages.happening:
Abraham gets up from beside his wife and speaks to the Hittites: “I am a foreigner and an outsider among you. Give me a burial site among you so that I can bury my dead” (verses 3-4).

They answer, “You are God’s chosen one among us. Bury your dead in the finest of our tombs” (verse 6). Abraham bows and asks them to approach Ephron son of Zohar for him, to sell him the cave of Machpelah at the end of Ephron's field, “for full price” (verses 7-9).

Ephron is sitting there at the city gate. He answers, “No, my lord. Listen to me. I give you the field, and I give you the cave that is in it” (verse 11). Abraham says he will pay the price (verse 13).

Ephron replies, “The land is worth four hundred shekels of silver, but what is that between you and me? Bury your dead” (verse 15). Abraham weighs out “four hundred shekels of silver, according to the standard of the merchants” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Abraham calls himself ‘a foreigner and an outsider’. That means a resident alien: someone allowed to live among a people and graze his flocks, but with no right to own land. After all those years in the land God promised him, Abraham owns none of it.

Who were these Hittites? The best-known Hittites ruled an empire far to the north, in what is now Turkey. Genesis 10:15 lists Heth among the descendants of Canaan, and the people here have local, Canaanite-sounding names like Ephron and Zohar. Many scholars think the Hittites of Hebron were a local people with a similar name. Others think there was some link with the north. It is not certain.

The whole deal is done at the city gate, in front of everyone. The gate was where business was done and witnessed. The people listening are the witnesses. That is why ‘in the presence of’ and ‘listen’ come again and again.

Listen to the polite bargaining. The Hittites offer their best tomb. Ephron offers the field as a gift. In that world such an offer was often a courteous opening, not meant to be taken. If Abraham took the land as a gift, someone could later say it was never really his. So he insists on paying full price.

Then Ephron names his price as if it were nothing: ‘what is that between you and me?’ Four hundred shekels was a large amount of silver. Silver was weighed, not counted; coins came much later. Many readers think Ephron named a high price and Abraham paid it without a word.

And notice the words ‘bury my dead’. They come back again and again. Under all the politeness is a grieving man who needs somewhere to put his wife.
passages.later:
Israel's law later reminded the people that the whole land belonged to God and that they too were ‘foreigners and residents’ with him (Leviticus 25:23). A psalm prays, “I am a foreigner dwelling with You, a stranger like all my fathers” (Psalm 39:12).

Peter writes to Christians “as foreigners and exiles” (1 Peter 2:11). Hebrews says of Abraham's family, “they acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth” (Hebrews 11:13).

Jeremiah, much later, bought a field “and I weighed out seventeen shekels of silver” (Jeremiah 32:9), a sign of hope that God would bring his people back.
passages.asks: Abraham was promised a whole land, and here he has to bargain and pay a high price for one grave in it. Ask whether you are waiting for a promise of God that you can see only a small piece of. Then notice that Abraham paid in full, and did not grab.

passages.t: A field, a cave, and Sarah's grave
passages.happening:
“So Ephron’s field at Machpelah near Mamre, the cave that was in it, and all the trees within the boundaries of the field were deeded over to Abraham’s possession in the presence of all the Hittites who had come to the gate of his city” (verses 17-18).

“After this, Abraham buried his wife Sarah in the cave of the field at Machpelah near Mamre (that is, Hebron) in the land of Canaan” (verse 19).

“So the field and its cave were deeded by the Hittites to Abraham as a burial site” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
The deal is spelled out like a legal record: the field, the cave, and even the trees inside its borders. Everyone at the gate is a witness. No one can ever say this field is not Abraham's.

The key word is ‘possession’. God promised Abraham the land ‘as an eternal possession’ (17:8). This field is the first piece of the land that Abraham legally owns. It is a grave. The only land Abraham ever owns in Canaan is a place to bury his dead. (See the note on 12:4-9 for what the land promise means.)

That was not defeat. It was faith. By burying Sarah in the land God promised, Abraham said that he believed the promise. His family would not go back to Haran. They belonged here, even in death.

The cave becomes the family grave. Abraham will be buried here (25:9), and later Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob and Leah (49:29-31; 50:13).

The traditional site of the cave is in Hebron today. A great stone wall built around it in the time of King Herod, about two thousand years ago, still stands. A church stood there in Byzantine times, and later a mosque. Jews, Christians and Muslims all honor the place, because all three remember Abraham. The Muslim name for it is al-Haram al-Ibrahimi, the sanctuary of Abraham. These notes make no claim about any modern dispute over the site.
passages.later:
Stephen reminds his hearers that God gave Abraham “no inheritance here, not even a foot of ground” (Acts 7:5). (In Acts 7:16 Stephen seems to join this purchase with Jacob's purchase at Shechem in Genesis 33:19. Many readers think he is summing up two stories in one sentence.)

Hebrews says Abraham's family “died in faith, without having received the things they were promised” (Hebrews 11:13), because “they were longing for a better country, a heavenly one” (Hebrews 11:16).

Jesus points to the people buried in this cave when he speaks of the resurrection. God said, “‘I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? He is not the God of the dead, but of the living” (Matthew 22:32).
passages.asks: Abraham's only land was a grave, and he bought it as if the whole promise were already true. Ask where you need to act on God's promise before you see it kept. Then remember Jesus' words: God is the God of the living.
